mainTopic: Can a person forbid what is not his through עבודה זרה (גוי versus Jew versus משומד), and a new משנה on where one may not slaughter
overview: Earlier on the daf, רב הונא ruled that someone who slaughters another person's animal for עבודה זרה makes it forbidden. רב נחמן, רב עמרם and רב יצחק disagreed, because אין אדם אוסר דבר שאינו שלו: a person cannot forbid something that is not his. The amud first explains that a person's own חטאת counts as his, because he gets atonement through it. It then answers two challenges from משניות by saying the person causing the harm was a partner. Next the גמרא shows that the same argument appears among the תנאים, in a ברייתא about a גוי pouring a Jew's wine as a libation. רב נחמן and his colleagues then give a new approach that fits even the stricter תנא: only a גוי forbids another's property, because a Jew who does this just wants to upset the owner. The two משניות are now explained as speaking about a ישראל משומד. רב אשי adds that a Jew who accepts a warning and goes ahead counts as the greatest משומד. Finally, a new משנה begins, listing places where one may not let the blood of a שחיטה flow, such as seas, rivers, vessels and a hole in the ground. Its reason for the marketplace rule continues on the next amud.

steps.title: But not an animal offering
steps.stepSummary: The end of the earlier statement: the case where all three prohibitions happen at once works only with a bird חטאת, not with an animal זבח.
steps.simpleTranslation: But with an animal offering, it does not work.
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes a statement from the previous part of the daf. The case where someone breaks three prohibitions at the same moment only works with a bird חטאת, not with an animal offering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The statement limits the case to a bird חטאת. The next step will ask why an animal חטאת would not work just as well. It asks this based on the view that a person cannot forbid what is not his.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal offering
A bird sin offering

phrases.english: But an animal offering, no.
phrases.notes: This finishes a statement that began earlier; it's talking about the bird חטאת case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the statement that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Breaking all three prohibitions at once works only with a bird חטאת, not with an animal offering.

steps.title: Why only a bird sin offering?
steps.stepSummary: If a person cannot forbid what is not his, an animal חטאת should also work, so why does the statement mention only a bird חטאת?
steps.simpleTranslation: And if a person cannot forbid something that is not his, why specifically a bird sin offering? Even an animal sin offering would also work!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the view of רב נחמן and his colleagues by using the statement it just finished. If they are right, an animal חטאת should also allow all three prohibitions at once.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A חטאת animal is no longer simply the owner's property, because the כהנים get to benefit from it. So if a person cannot forbid what is not his, cutting the first סימן for עבודה זרה would not make the animal forbidden. The slaughter could then continue and break all three prohibitions together. The fact that the statement says only a bird works suggests that the owner does make the animal forbidden right away.

keyTerms.term: אֵין אָדָם אוֹסֵר דָּבָר שֶׁאֵינוֹ שֶׁלּוֹ
keyTerms.meaning: A person cannot make forbidden something that does not belong to him
Why specifically this case?
An animal sin offering

phrases.english: And if a person does not render forbidden
an item that is not his,
why specifically a bird sin offering?
Even an animal sin offering as well!
phrases.notes: Because the כהנים benefit from a חטאת, it is not fully the owner's. So in this view his first cut would not forbid it.

steps.triggerLanguage: ואי אין אדם אוסר דבר שאינו שלו מאי איריא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the limit in Step 1 to attack the view that a person cannot forbid what is not his.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view of רב נחמן, רב עמרם and רב יצחק that אין אדם אוסר דבר שאינו שלו
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a person cannot forbid what is not his, an animal חטאת would work just like a bird. Limiting the case to a bird implies the owner does forbid it.

steps.title: Acquired for atonement counts as his
steps.stepSummary: Since the owner acquires the חטאת to get atonement from it, it is treated as his own, so he does make it forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since he acquires it for his atonement, it is considered like his own.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the owner's connection to his חטאת is strong enough to count as ownership. He receives atonement through it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer does not give up the rule that a person cannot forbid what is not his. It explains that a חטאת counts as the owner's for this purpose. So his first cut for עבודה זרה forbids the animal, and all three prohibitions cannot happen together.

keyTerms.meaning: He acquires it for his atonement
It is considered like his own

phrases.english: Since he acquires it for atonement
it is like his own.

steps.triggerLanguage: כיון דקניא ליה לכפרה כדידיה דמיא
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining ownership: the owner's link to the offering counts as ownership
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A חטאת is not the owner's, so he could not forbid it.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because he gains atonement from it, it counts as his, so he does forbid it with the first cut.
steps.whatToRemember: A person's own קרבן counts as 'his' for making it forbidden, because he gets atonement through it.

steps.title: Two people holding one knife
steps.stepSummary: A source teaches that if two people slaughter together and one has a forbidden intention, the slaughter is invalid. This seems to show that someone can forbid an animal that is not his.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: two people hold a knife and slaughter. One slaughters for one of the forbidden things listed, and one slaughters for a proper purpose. The slaughter is invalid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new challenge from the משנה. The person with the bad intention is not described as the owner, yet he still ruins the slaughter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה does not say that the person with the forbidden intention owns the animal. If his intention invalidates it anyway, it looks like a person can forbid what is not his, which goes against רב נחמן and his colleagues.

keyTerms.meaning: Holding the knife together
For the sake of, with the intention of
The slaughter is invalid

phrases.english: Come and hear:
two people are grasping a knife and slaughtering,
one for the sake of one of all those,
phrases.notes: 'All those' means the forbidden things listed earlier in the משנה, like mountains, hills and other things people worship.

phrases.english: and one for the sake of a proper matter —
his slaughter is invalid.

steps.triggerLanguage: תא שמע שנים אוחזין בסכין ושוחטין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge against the same view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that אין אדם אוסר דבר שאינו שלו
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Someone who is not described as the owner still makes the animal invalid, so a person can apparently forbid what is not his.

steps.title: He was a partner
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is talking about a case where the person with the forbidden intention owns a share of the animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are we dealing with here? A case where he has a share in the animal as a partner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by narrowing the case. The person with the bad intention is a part owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he owns part of the animal, he is forbidding something that is partly his own. That fits the rule that a person cannot forbid what is not his, so the challenge falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)
Partnership, a share of ownership
In it

phrases.english: Here, with what are we dealing?
Where he has a partnership in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: הכא במאי עסקינן דאית ליה שותפות בגוה
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the source to a specific case (partnership)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The person with the bad intention was a stranger to the animal.
steps.terutzMaskana: He was a partner, so he forbade something that was partly his.

steps.title: Causing damage by making things forbidden
steps.stepSummary: A משנה makes a person pay if he deliberately makes someone else's food טמא, mixes in תרומה, or pours the wine as a libation. This assumes he really did forbid another person's property.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: one who makes something טמא, one who mixes in תרומה, and one who pours wine as a libation: if by accident, he is exempt; if on purpose, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another source against רב נחמן's view. The person who pours someone else's wine for עבודה זרה must pay, which means the wine really became forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Payment is due only if real damage happened. If the libation forbids the owner's wine, then a person can forbid what is not his.

keyTerms.meaning: One who makes someone else's food ritually impure
One who mixes תרומה into someone else's ordinary produce, making it forbidden to non-כהנים
One who pours someone else's wine as a libation to עבודה זרה
By accident / on purpose

phrases.english: Come and hear:
one who renders impure, one who mixes in teruma, and one who pours a libation —
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in גיטין 52b, about damaging another person's produce or wine.

phrases.english: unwittingly, he is exempt; intentionally, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third challenge against the same view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that אין אדם אוסר דבר שאינו שלו
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: He must pay for pouring another person's wine, so the wine really became forbidden even though it was not his.

steps.title: Here too, a partner
steps.stepSummary: The same answer: the one who did the damage owns a share of the produce or wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, it is a case where he has a share in it as a partner.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the same answer as before. The person who caused the damage was a part owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since he owns part of it, he can forbid the whole thing. He pays his partner for the partner's lost share. The rule that a person cannot forbid what is not his remains in place.

keyTerms.meaning: Here too, the same answer applies

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא נָמֵי דְּאִית לֵיהּ שׁוּתָּפוּת בְּגַוַּהּ.
phrases.english: Here too, where he has a partnership in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: הכא נמי דאית ליה שותפות בגוה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 6 the same way Step 5 answered Step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the source to a specific case (partnership)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He damaged property that belonged entirely to someone else.
steps.terutzMaskana: He was a partner, so he forbade something that was partly his own.
steps.whatToRemember: Every proof that a person can forbid another's property is answered the same way: the person was a partner.

steps.title: The same argument among the תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The argument between רב הונא and the others matches a ברייתא about a גוי who poured a Jew's wine as a libation. The anonymous first view forbids the wine. רבי יהודה בן בתירא and רבי יהודה בן בבא permit it for two reasons, the second being that a person cannot forbid someone else's wine against his will.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like a dispute between תנאים: a גוי who poured a Jew's wine as a libation, but not in front of an idol, has made it forbidden. רבי יהודה בן בתירא and רבי יהודה בן בבא permit it for two reasons. First, people pour wine as a libation only in front of an idol. Second, the Jew can say to him: 'It is not in your power to forbid my wine against my will.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the argument about forbidding someone else's property already appears among the תנאים. The first view matches רב הונא, and the dissenting view matches רב נחמן and his colleagues.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first view says the גוי forbade the Jew's wine, so a person can forbid what is not his. The second reason of the dissenting רבנן, 'it is not in your power to forbid my wine,' is exactly the idea of אין אדם אוסר דבר שאינו שלו. Both sides of the argument among the אמוראים therefore have support from תנאים.

keyTerms.meaning: This matches a dispute among the תנאים
Poured wine as a libation for עבודה זרה
In front of an idol
It is not in your power
Against my will

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that רב הונא and the other אמוראים are not making up a new argument. They are continuing a disagreement that already existed among the תנאים.
steps.confusionAlert: The dissenting רבנן give two separate reasons. Only the second one, 'not in your power,' connects to our question of forbidding another person's property. The first reason is about the wine not being poured in front of an idol.

phrases.english: Like a dispute of tanna'im:
a gentile who poured a Jew's wine as a libation
not in the presence of an idol — has rendered it forbidden.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בְּתֵירָא וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן בָּבָא
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
permit it because of two reasons:
one — that people do not pour wine as a libation
except in the presence of an idol,
and one — that he can say to him:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the Jewish owner, speaking to the גוי.

phrases.english: 'It is not entirely in your power
to forbid my wine against my will.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending the view of רב נחמן against all the challenges, the גמרא shows that the whole argument goes back to the תנאים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first view in the ברייתא holds that a גוי can forbid a Jew's wine. רבי יהודה בן בתירא and רבי יהודה בן בבא hold that a person cannot forbid another's property against his will.
steps.whatToRemember: The question of whether a person can forbid what is not his is an argument among the תנאים: the first view of the ברייתא matches רב הונא, and the two רבי יהודהs match רב נחמן, רב עמרם and רב יצחק.

steps.title: A Jew only means to upset the owner
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן, רב עמרם and רב יצחק say that even according to the view that a person can forbid what is not his, this applies only to a גוי. A Jew who does it is just trying to hurt the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב נחמן, רב עמרם and רב יצחק say: Even according to the one who says a person can forbid an item that is not his, that is only said about a גוי. But a Jew is really just trying to upset the owner.
steps.whatsHappening: Three אמוראים give their own approach. They say a Jew cannot forbid someone else's animal or wine, even according to the strict view in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 8, the argument seemed to depend on the ברייתא's two views. These אמוראים say their position works even with the strict view. The reason is that a גוי really means to serve his idol. A Jew who does this to someone else's property is not truly worshipping. He just wants to hurt the owner, so his act does not count as עבודה זרה.

keyTerms.meaning: A person can make forbidden an item that does not belong to him
This applies only to... (limits the rule)
He intends to cause him pain / upset him

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with the earlier answer in steps 5 and 7. There, the answer was that he owned a share. Here is a completely different approach, based on what a Jew really intends.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a new standard: what the person intends decides whether the act forbids the item. The rest of this section tests that standard.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב נַחְמָן וְרַב עַמְרָם וְרַב יִצְחָק אָמְרִי:
phrases.english: And Rav Nachman, Rav Amram, and Rav Yitzchak say:
Even according to the one who says
that a person can forbid an item that is not his,
this applies only to a gentile,
but a Jew intends only to upset him.
phrases.notes: "Him" means the owner of the animal or wine.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב נַחְמָן וְרַב עַמְרָם וְרַב יִצְחָק אָמְרִי: אֲפִילּוּ לְמַאן דְּאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different explanation that fits even the strict view in the ברייתא of step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only a גוי forbids another person's item through עבודה זרה. A Jew is assumed to be acting only to upset the owner.

steps.title: Challenge from two people holding one knife
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says that if two people slaughter together and one has an idolatrous intention, the slaughter is invalid. That seems to show a Jew can forbid an animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If two people hold a knife and slaughter, one for the sake of one of those listed things and one for a proper purpose, the slaughter is invalid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back the משנה from step 4 to challenge the new approach. In that משנה, a Jew's bad intention does make the animal forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה is speaking about Jews slaughtering. One of them has a forbidden intention, and the shared animal still becomes invalid. So a Jew's intention seems to count, and he is not just trying to upset someone.

keyTerms.meaning: Holding a knife (two people slaughtering together)
For the sake of (the intention while slaughtering)
His slaughter is invalid

phrases.aramaic: תָּא שְׁמַע: שְׁנַיִם אוֹחֲזִין בְּסַכִּין וְשׁוֹחֲטִין,
phrases.english: Come and hear: Two people holding a knife and slaughtering,
one for the sake of one of all these,
phrases.notes: "All these" is the list earlier in the משנה, things like mountains and hills.

phrases.english: and one for the sake of a proper purpose,
the slaughter is invalid.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: שְׁנַיִם אוֹחֲזִין בְּסַכִּין וְשׁוֹחֲטִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the view in step 9 using the משנה from step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a Jew only intends to upset the owner and does not forbid the animal.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the משנה, a Jew's idolatrous intention makes the animal invalid. That shows a Jew's intention does count.

steps.title: The משנה is about a Jewish transgressor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה is talking about a ישראל משומד, who really does mean to serve the idol.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are we dealing with here? With a Jew who is a משומד.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the view of רב נחמן and his colleagues. It limits the משנה to a Jew who has turned to idol worship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A משומד really means to worship, just like a גוי. So his intention counts and forbids the animal. A regular Jew is still assumed to be only trying to upset the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)
A Jew who has abandoned the Torah (here, one who serves idols)

phrases.english: What are we dealing with here?
With a Jewish transgressor.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the source to a specific case (אוקימתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to be about any Jew.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a משומד, whose intention to worship is real.

steps.title: Challenge from paying for ruined food or wine
steps.stepSummary: A משנה makes a person pay if he deliberately makes someone's food טמא, mixes in תרומה, or pours someone's wine as a libation. That suggests a Jew really does forbid another person's wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: One who makes food טמא, one who mixes in תרומה, and one who pours wine as a libation: if by accident, he is exempt. If on purpose, he must pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back the משנה from step 6 to challenge the new approach. The משנה treats a Jew who pours another's wine as having truly made it forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The libation-pourer has to pay for the wine. That only makes sense if the wine really became forbidden. So it seems a Jew can forbid someone else's wine.

keyTerms.meaning: One who makes someone else's food ritually impure
One who mixes תרומה into someone else's ordinary food, forbidding it to non-כהנים
One who pours someone else's wine as an offering to an idol
By accident / on purpose

phrases.english: Come and hear: One who makes impure, one who mixes in terumah, and one who pours as a libation,
phrases.notes: This is the same משנה from step 6. The food or wine belongs to someone else.

phrases.english: if unintentionally, he is exempt,
if intentionally, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to step 9, this time using the משנה from step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a Jew does not forbid another person's wine.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The pourer must pay for the loss. That assumes the wine truly became forbidden through a Jew's libation.

steps.title: This too is about a Jewish transgressor
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives the same answer: the משנה is about a ישראל משומד.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, it is talking about a Jew who is a משומד.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the second challenge the same way as the first. The wine-pourer in that משנה is a משומד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A משומד truly means to worship, so his libation really forbids the wine, and he must pay. A regular Jew would be assumed to be just upsetting the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Here too (the same answer applies)

steps.whatToRemember: Under this approach, only a גוי or a ישראל משומד can forbid someone else's item through עבודה זרה. A regular Jew is assumed to be only upsetting the owner.

phrases.english: Here too, it is a Jewish transgressor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 12 the same way step 11 answered step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the source to a specific case (אוקימתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to be about any Jew who pours wine.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is about a משומד, whose libation is real worship.

steps.title: What if he was warned and accepted the warning?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרבא asks רב אשי about a regular Jew who was warned and accepted the warning. Does he forbid the animal?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא, son of רבא, said to רב אשי: If they warned him and he accepted the warning, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: A new question tests the line between a regular Jew and a משומד. What about a Jew who was clearly warned and went ahead anyway?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The assumption that a Jew only wants to upset the owner may not hold here. He has openly accepted a warning that this is a sin punishable by death. The question is whether that turns him into someone whose act really counts as worship.

keyTerms.meaning: They warned him (that the act is forbidden and punishable)
He accepted the warning, saying he is doing it anyway, knowing the punishment
What is the law?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Acha, son of Rava, said to Rav Ashi:

phrases.aramaic: הִתְרוּ בּוֹ וְקִבֵּל עָלָיו הַתְרָאָה, מַאי?
phrases.english: If they warned him and he accepted the warning, what is the law?
phrases.notes: 'Him' is a regular Jew, not a משומד, who announced he was slaughtering someone else's animal for idols.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי: הִתְרוּ בּוֹ וְקִבֵּל עָלָיו הַתְרָאָה, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Probes the edge of the משומד category set up in steps 11 and 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a regular Jew who accepts a warning count like a משומד, so that he forbids the animal?

steps.title: No greater transgressor than that
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that a person who accepts the warning has given himself over to death. He is the greatest משומד, so he certainly forbids the animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Are you talking about someone who gave himself over to death? You have no greater משומד than this.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the question. Accepting the warning makes the person a full משומד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone who goes ahead after hearing that the act carries the death penalty is not just playing a prank on the owner. He is truly committed to the sin. So he is treated as a משומד, and his act forbids the animal.

keyTerms.meaning: He gave himself over to death (by accepting the warning)
There is none greater than this

steps.whatToRemember: A משומד is not only someone known as an idol worshipper. A Jew who accepts a warning and goes ahead also counts as a משומד, and his act forbids the item.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הִתִּיר עַצְמוֹ לְמִיתָה קָאָמְרַתְּ?
phrases.english: He said to him: You are speaking of one who gave himself over to death?
You have no transgressor greater than this.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הִתִּיר עַצְמוֹ לְמִיתָה קָאָמְרַתְּ? אֵין לָךְ מְשׁוּמָּד גָּדוֹל מִזֶּה
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Accepting the warning makes him the greatest משומד, so he forbids the animal.

steps.title: Slaughtering into seas, rivers, and vessels
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says you may not let the blood of a slaughtered animal flow into seas, rivers, or vessels. You may slaughter into a round pit of water, and on a ship you may slaughter onto vessels.
steps.simpleTranslation: MISHNA: You may not slaughter so that the blood flows into seas, into rivers, or into vessels. But you may slaughter into a round pit of water. And on a ship, you may slaughter onto vessels.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה opens with a list of places where you must not let the blood of a שחיטה flow, and then gives the allowed options.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה itself gives no reason here, but these are ways idol worshippers slaughtered, so doing it looks like עבודה זרה. A round pit of water is allowed, and so is slaughtering onto vessels on a ship. There it is clear the person only wants to keep the ship clean.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה, the opening text the גמרא will discuss
Seas
Rivers
Vessels or containers
A round pit or dug-out circle
A ship

steps.confusionAlert: Slaughtering into vessels is forbidden in general, but on a ship it is allowed. The ship is a special case where the reason for using a vessel is obvious.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One may not slaughter, neither into seas
nor into rivers
nor into vessels
But one may slaughter
into a round pit of water
And on a ship, onto vessels
phrases.notes: He means that on a ship you may let the blood run onto vessels, so the ship doesn't get dirty.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ אֵין שׁוֹחֲטִין לֹא לְתוֹךְ יַמִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion about a ישראל משומד ended at step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may not let the blood flow into seas, rivers, or vessels. One may slaughter into a round pit of water, and onto vessels on a ship.

steps.title: Slaughtering into a small hole in the ground
steps.stepSummary: The משנה forbids slaughtering into a small hole at all. But it allows making a hole inside your house to catch the blood, though not in the marketplace.
steps.simpleTranslation: You may not slaughter into a small hole at all. But a person may make a small hole inside his house so the blood will flow into it. And in the marketplace he may not do this, so that he will not...
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds another forbidden place, a small hole in the ground, and then gives an exception for inside your own house. The sentence explaining the marketplace rule continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Slaughtering into a hole is forbidden in general, since that also looks like idol worship. Inside your house, a hole is fine because people can see it is only there to keep the house clean. In the public marketplace it is not allowed, and the משנה is about to give the reason.

keyTerms.meaning: A small hole or pit dug in the ground
At all, in any way
Marketplace, a public place

steps.confusionAlert: The same hole is forbidden in one place and allowed in another. What matters is where it is (your house or the public marketplace) and how it looks to others.

phrases.english: One may not slaughter into a small hole at all
but one may make a small hole inside his house
so that the blood will enter into it
And in the marketplace one may not do so
so that he will not

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same משנה with another forbidden place, a hole in the ground, and its exception.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Slaughtering into a small hole is forbidden. Making a hole inside one's house to catch the blood is allowed, but not in the marketplace.
